source_text: Quibus duobus dominis neget posse seruiri, quia alterum offendi sit necesse alterum defendi, ipse declarat, deum proponens et mamonam. proinde mamonam quem intellegi uelit, si interpretem non habes, ab ipso potes discere. admonens enim nos de saecularibus suffragia nobis prospicere amicitiarum secundum serui illius exemplum, qui ab actu summotus dominicos debitores diminutis cautionibus releuat in subsidium sibi: et ego, inquit, dico uobis, facite uobis amicos de mamona iniustitiae, de nummo scilicet, de ' quo et seruus ille. iniustitiae enim auctorem et dominatorem totius saeculi nummum scimus omnes. cui famulatam uidens Pharisaeorum cupiditatem ammentauit hanc sententiam: non potestis deo seruire et mamonae. inridebant denique Pharisaei pecuniae cupidi, quod intellexissent scilicet mamonam de nummo dictum, ne quia existimet in mamona creatorem intellegendum et Christum a creatoris illos seruitute reuocasse.. quid nunc? potius ex hoc disce unum a Christo deum ostensum. duos enim dominos nominauit, deum et mamonam, crea. torem et nummum: denique non potestis deo seruire, utique ei, cui uidebantur seruire, et mamonam, cui magis destinabantur. quodsi ipse alium se ageret, non duos dominos, sed tres demonstrasset — et creator enim dominus, quia deus, et utique magis dominus quam mamonas magisque homini obseruandus, qua magis dominus —; quale est enim, ut qui mamonam dominum dixerat et cum domino iunxerat uero, ipsum dominum taceret, id est deum creatorem? aut numquid tacendo eo concessit seruiendum ei esse, si solummodo sibi et mamonae negauit posse seruiri? ita cum unum deum ponit, nominaturus et creatorem, si alius esset ipse, creatorem nominauit quem [dominum] sine alio [deo non] posuit. et illud itaque relucebit, quomodo dictum sit: (si) in mamona iniusto fideles non extitistis, quod uerum est quis uobis credet? in nummo scilicet iniusto, non in creatore, quem et Marcion iustum facit, et: si in alieno fideles inuenti non estis, meum quis dabit uobis? alienum enim debet esse a semis dei quod iniustum est. creator autem quomodo alienus erat Pharisaeis, proprius deus Iudaicae gentis? si ergo haec non cadunt in creatorem, sed in mamonam, 'quis uobis credet quod uerius est'? et 'quis uobis dabit quod meum est'? non potest quasi ali{en)us dixisse de alterius dei gratia. tunc enim uideretur ita dixisse, si eos in creatorem, non in mamonam infideles notando per creatoris mentionem distinctione se fecisset dei alterius, non commissuri suam ueritatem infidelibus creatoris, t quoniam tunc alterius uideri potest, si non ad hoc proponatur, ut a re, de qua agitur, separetur. Si autem et iustificantes se coram hominibus Pharisaei spem mercedis in homine ponebant, illo eos sensu increpabat, quo et propheta Hieremias: miser homo, qui spem habet in homine. si et adicit: scit autem deus corda uestra, illius dei uim commemorabat, (qui) lucernam se pronuntiarat scrutantem renes et corda. si superbiam tangit: quod elatum est apud homines perosum est deo, Esaiam ponit ante oculos: dies enim domini Sabaoth in omnem contumeliosum et superbum, in omnem sublimem et elatum, et humiliabuntur. Possum iam colligere, cur tanto aeuo deus Marcionis fuerit in occulto. expectabat, opinor, donec haec omnia disceret a creatore. didicit igitur usque ad Iohannis tempora atque ita exinde processit adnuntiare regnum dei dicens: lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem; ex quo regnum dei adnuntiatur. quasi non et nos limitem quendam agnoscamus Iohannem constitutum inter uetera et noua, ad quem desineret Iudaismus et a quo inciperet Christianismus, non tamen, ut ab alia uirtute facta sit sedatio legis et prophetarum et initiatio euangelii, in quo est dei regnum.' [Christus ipse.] nam id si probauimus, et uetera transitura et noua successura praedicari a creatore, si et Iohannes antecursor et praeparator ostenditur uiarum domini euangelium', superducturi et regnum dei promulgaturi, et ex hoc iam, quod Iohannes uenit, ipse erit Christus qui Iohannem erit subsecutus ut antecursorem; et, si desierunt uetera et coeperunt ! noua interstite Iohanne, non erit mirum quod ex dispositione est creatoris, ut unde(unde) magis probetur ** quam ex legis et prophetarum in Iohannem occasu et exinde ortu regni dei. transeat igitur caelum et terra citius, sicut et lex et: prophetae, quam unus apexuerborum domini-nerbum enim, inquit Esaias, dei nostri manet in aeuum —: nam quoniam in Esaia iam tunc Christus, sermo scilicet et spiritus creatoris, Iohannem praedicarat — uocem clamantis in deserto: parate uiam domini — in hoc uenturum, ut legis et] prophetarum ordo exinde cessaret, per adimpletionem, non per destructionem, et regnum dei a Christo adnuntiaretur, I ideo subtexuit facilius elementa transitura quam uerba sua,' confirmans hoc quoque, quod de Iohanne dixerat, non praeterisse.
pass_a_gloss: To whom He says that two lords cannot be served, because it is necessary that one offend the other, and defend the other, He Himself declares, setting forth God and mammon. Therefore, mammon, which He wishes to be understood, if you do not have an interpreter, you can learn from Him Himself. For, admonishing us to look out for worldly friendships, according to the example of that servant, who, having been removed from office, relieves his master's debtors by diminishing their securities, for his own benefit: and I, He says, say to you, make friends for yourselves from mammon of injustice, namely from money, from which also that servant. For we know that money is the author and ruler of all worldly injustice. Seeing the covetousness of the Pharisees, He strengthened this statement: you cannot serve God and mammon. Finally, the Pharisees, who were greedy for money, ridiculed, because they understood that mammon was spoken of in terms of money, not because they thought that the creator was to be understood in mammon, and that Christ had recalled them from the service of the creator. What now? Rather, learn from this that one God is shown by Christ. For He named two lords, God and mammon, the creator and money: finally, you cannot serve God, certainly to Him, whom they seemed to serve, and mammon, to whom they were more devoted. But if He Himself were acting as another, He would have demonstrated not two lords, but three — and the creator is indeed the Lord, because He is God, and certainly a greater Lord than mammon, and more to be observed by man, because He is a greater Lord —; what kind of thing is it, that He who said mammon was Lord, and joined it with the Lord, would be silent about the Lord Himself, that is, the creator God? Or did He, by being silent, concede that He should be served, if only He had denied that He and mammon could be served? Thus, when He sets forth one God, He names the creator, if He Himself were another, He would have named the creator, whom He did not set forth as another Lord. And this will also become clear, how it was said: if you have not been faithful in mammon of injustice, what is true, who will trust you? certainly in unjust money, not in the creator, whom even Marcion makes just, and: if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is mine? For what is another's must be unjust, and separate from the semi-god. But how was the creator alien to the Pharisees, when He was the proper God of the Jewish people? If, therefore, these things do not fall upon the creator, but upon mammon, who will trust you, what is more true? And who will give you what is mine? He cannot have said this as if it were another's God's gift. For then He would have seemed to say this, if He had noted them as unfaithful in the creator, not in mammon, by mentioning the creator, making a distinction between the other God, not entrusting His truth to the unfaithful of the creator. But if the Pharisees, justifying themselves before men, were putting their hope of reward in men, He was rebuking them with the same sense as the prophet Jeremiah: woe to the man who puts his hope in man. And if He adds: but God knows your hearts, He was commemorating the power of that God, who had declared Himself to be the searcher of kidneys and hearts. If He touches on pride: what is exalted among men is an abomination to God, He sets Isaiah before their eyes: for the day of the Lord of hosts will be upon every arrogant and proud man, and they will be humbled. I can now gather why the God of Marcion was in hiding for so long. He was waiting, I think, until He had learned all these things from the creator. Therefore, He learned up to the time of John, and thus proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying: the law and the prophets were until John; from whom the kingdom of God is announced. As if we also do not recognize a certain boundary established by John between the old and the new, from which Judaism ceased and Christianity began, not, however, that the cessation of the law and the prophets, and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, was made by another virtue, but by Christ Himself. For if we have proven this, that the old things are passing away and the new things are succeeding, as predicted by the creator, and John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord, and the gospel, and the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and from this, now that John has come, He Himself will be Christ, who will follow John as a forerunner; and if the old things have ceased and the new things have begun, with John in between, it will not be surprising that this is from the disposition of the creator, so that it may be proven more than from the passing away of the law and the prophets in John, and from then on, the rising of the kingdom of God. Therefore, let heaven and earth pass away more quickly, just as the law and the prophets, than one dot of the Lord's words — for the word of our God remains forever —; for since in Isaiah, Christ, namely the speech and spirit of the creator, had already predicted John, saying: a voice crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord — in this, that the order of the law and the prophets would cease from then on, through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ. Therefore, He more easily undermined the elements that would pass away than His own words, confirming also what He had said about John, that He had not passed away.

choices.why: The context suggests that mammon refers to wealth or riches.
The term deus is used to refer to the one true God.
The term creator is used to refer to God as the creator of the world.

If you have not been faithful in mammon of injustice, who will trust you?
A voice crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord

pass_b_english: Jesus declares that you cannot serve two masters, because serving one inevitably offends the other; He names them: God and mammon (Luke 16:13). If you lack an interpreter for what He means by mammon, you can learn it straight from Him. He warns us to secure our future through worldly friendships, citing the shrewd manager who, once fired, cut his master's debtors' bills to buy their favor. "I tell you," He says, "make friends for yourselves with the mammon of injustice — that is, with money, the very stuff that manager used" (Luke 16:11). Everyone knows money is the author and ruler of all worldly injustice. When the money-loving Pharisees sneered, Jesus doubled down: you cannot serve God and mammon. They mocked Him because they realized He was talking about cash, not because they thought He was identifying the Creator with mammon and recalling them from the Creator's service. So learn this instead: Christ reveals one God. He names two lords — God and mammon, the Creator and money — and says you cannot serve God, the very One the Pharisees claimed to serve, and mammon, the one they actually served. If Jesus were some other deity, He would have presented three lords, not two — for the Creator is Lord by virtue of being God, a far greater Lord than mammon, and far more binding on humanity. What kind of logic would have Jesus call mammon a lord, pair it with the Lord, and then fall silent about the Lord Himself, the Creator God? Or did His silence concede that the Creator deserves service, simply because He denied that He and mammon could be served together? By positing one God and naming the Creator, Jesus shows He is not another god; if He were, He would have named the Creator as a separate lord, which He did not. This also clarifies His words: "If you have not been faithful with the mammon of injustice, who will trust you with what is true?" — meaning unjust money, not the Creator, whom even Marcion calls just. And: "If you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is mine?" (Luke 16:11). What belongs to another must be unjust and alien to the demiurge. But how was the Creator alien to the Pharisees, when He was the proper God of the Jewish nation? If these charges land on mammon, not the Creator, then "who will trust you with what is more true? And who will give you what is mine?" Jesus could not have spoken as if dispensing another god's gift; that would only make sense if He had indicted them for unfaithfulness to the Creator, not mammon, and used the Creator's mention to distinguish a rival God — refusing to entrust His truth to the Creator's unfaithful. Since the Pharisees justified themselves before men and pinned their hope of reward on human approval, Jesus rebuked them with the same force as Jeremiah: "Wretched is the man who puts his hope in man." When He adds, "But God knows your hearts," He invokes the power of that God who declared Himself the searcher of kidneys and hearts. When He strikes at pride — "What is exalted among men is an abomination to God" — He sets Isaiah before their eyes: "The day of the Lord of Hosts will come upon every arrogant and proud man, upon everyone lifted high, and they will be humbled." I can now see why Marcion's god stayed hidden so long: he was waiting, I suppose, to learn all this from the Creator. He studied up to John's time, then launched his announcement of God's kingdom: "The Law and the Prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed." As if we do not also recognize John as the boundary between old and new, where Judaism ended and Christianity began — not because another power effected the Law's cessation and the Gospel's inception, but Christ Himself. If we have proven that the old passes and the new succeeds by the Creator's prediction, and John is shown as the forerunner and preparer of the Lord's ways, the Gospel, and the kingdom's proclamation, then from John's arrival it follows that Jesus is the Christ who follows John as forerunner. And if the old ceased and the new began with John as the hinge, it is no surprise this flows from the Creator's own design — so that it is proven even more decisively by the Law and Prophets' sunset in John and the kingdom's sunrise thereafter than by any other means. Therefore let heaven and earth pass away sooner than one dot of the Lord's words — "The word of our God stands forever" —; for in Isaiah, Christ, the Word and Spirit of the Creator, had already foretold John: "A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord" (Isaiah 40:3) — signaling that the order of Law and Prophets would cease from that point through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ. That is why He made the passing elements easier to dismantle than His own words, confirming that what He said about John had not failed.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the identity of the Creator and the nature of Mammon. Scripture citations (Luke 16:13, Luke 16:11, Isaiah 40:3) are correctly applied to the relevant Latin clauses. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin.

Pass A: 'Quibus duobus dominis neget posse seruiri, quia alterum offendi sit necesse alterum defendi, ipse declarat, deum proponens et mamonam.' Pass B: 'Jesus declares that you cannot serve two masters, because serving one inevitably offends the other; He names them: God and mammon (Luke 16:13).'
